newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Jan PPI slides 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Jan PPI slides 0.3 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported the January Producer Price Index (PPI) fell 0.3 percent compared to a revised 0.6 percent jump in December.
Minus food and energy, the index was unchanged against a revised 0.1 percent increase the previous month. Economists had expected an overall PPI rise of 0.3 percent.
TIM ROGERS, ECONOMIST, TECHNICAL DATA, BOSTON: "What we're really seeing is a continuation of what we've been seeing for a long time ... very encouraging news at the wholesale level."
Rogers was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

KEVIN FLANAGAN, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "The figure is far more friendly than anyone would have forecasted and the (U.S. Treasury) market is embracing this information.
"The message is that the Federal Reserve will be in no hurry to raise rates immediately. The bottom line is that inflation at the wholesale level is basically quite negligible," he added.

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "It was a surprisingly soft number with food being a lot weaker. There was some strength in the energy sector with crude oil up sharply, but generally this was a strong number suggesting inflation was subdued."

ALISON LYNN REASER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BARNETT BANK INC: "It's very positive news for the bond market, especially the core index remaining totally flat, despite the fact that industrial activity had started to pick up at the end of 1996.

Reaser continued: "It is consistent with some of the recent signs of some moderation in the factory sector, with vendor performance showing that companies are not having any difficulties obtaining supplies. As a result, it appears that the economy is not showing price pressures from the commodities side as 1997 begins."

FREDERICK BREIMYER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, STATE STREET BANK: "This is an excellent number. It obviously beats expectations by quite a bit. Technically, we've got new seasonal factors in place, so things look a little different.

Breimyer went on: "Consumer foods and energy contributed to this decline. With energy, it was a timing issue. We thought prices would come off, but we had it in February, not January. Food is going to go the other way in February, with bad weather bringing short-term disruptions in food delivery.
"The report was very good without question, but we're in a process where crude and intermediate increases will start to move into finished goods prices," he added.

ANTHONY CHAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANC ONE INVESTMENT ADVISORS: "Energy brought the number down ... There was a little surprise on the cars where prices were so weak. The heavy trucks and the passenger car declines were a little weak. The reason the market's reaction is relatively subdued to these good final numbers is that people were looking at the core numbers. Because the pipeline costs were higher, the reaction is likely to be muted. The market should be celebrating, but the initial subdued reaction is (due) to the fact that you are not getting as much progress on the pipeline pressures. The pipeline pressures tell you where you're going.

JOSEPH LIRO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CIBC WOOD GUNDY SECURITIES INC: "Obviously the (Treasury) bond market responded very favorably to the intitial headline prints ... Now, the earlier stages of production of the story isn't as quite as favorable. We're getting a steady stream of increases in the intermediate goods sector and crude goods jumped 5.2 percent, and even excluding food and energy, they jumped 2.0 percent ... So, while the finished goods numbers are just extraordinarily positive, there's a little bit of pressure starting to be manifested at the earlier stages of production."
